The story was forgettable, but the philosophical ruminations were interesting.

I found the book profound and transformative. Everything that follows is personal opinion and experience, and I make no pretense whatsoever of correctness.

Understanding that our narrator is a singular conscious entity that has been housed inside two personalities is meaningful in the way that it illustrates that the faculties of our mental functions are no different than our limbs: they are experiences provided by accessory body parts. It has long been assumed and expounded upon that the mind has some sort of ethereal, complete presence, that is fundamentally unaffected by the loss of limbs or "secondary flesh". Who among us would contend that a man whose hand has been cut off is fundamentally a "new human being", compared to the one who had the whole body plus-hand before? To illustrate memory, preference, personality and individuality as mutable expressions of "brain-limbs" that can be altered without reducing the "magnitude of consciousness" in the individual is profoundly meaningful to me, personally.

I think a critical element of the book that pulled me in was the distinction between what a shim "means" and what a shim "is". An aluminum can's wall is an ideal shim, but his dear friend was incapable of seeing it that way, himming and hawwing until they turned back to seek a BMW-authorized shim to fix the problem.

I feel, due to various expressions of philosophy and personal experiences, that the conscious entity within us all is identical. It lives exclusively in the present moment, and it is capable of experience. "Memory", therefore, is the capability of the body to impose experiences on the presently-living, brand-new, unaltered conscious spark that lives equally within us all. This is no different than the way in which touching a surface with one's fingers imposes an experience upon the conscious spark. Just as a bodily limb touches a surface, and then enforces an experience on its conscious spark, so too do the hippocampus and amygdala enforce experiences based on physical fact.

Where limbs provide my conscious spark with experiences derived from their present moments, so does my amygdala provide experiences derived from my past. I am not "my past self"--after all, from a purely physics-based perspective, no such continuity exists. The whole of my body's matter has been replaced, even though the shape of it remains the same, just in such a way that a persistent whirlpool in a turn of a river remains present even though the molecules of water that compose it change from moment to moment. My amygdala performs a feat of symbolic representation. Being stimulated in this way, or that, it offers up experiences far greater in 'magnitude of data' than the input of my fingertips. But where my fingertips coarsely provide me input from billions upon billions of atoms, my amygdala provides detailed input from minute, tiny pieces of matter--nucleotides, surface receptors, and so on--magnified and extrapolated upon to produce wildly varying experiences, of smells, textures, flashes of visual form.

This illusion of continuity holds for the entirety of my life. So too it holds for the entirety of the lives of those all around me. This provides a comfortable illusion of a continuum, of a series of events that all happen "to me". Phaedrus, the dearly departed "past self" of our narrator, stands in a ghostly, un-knowable form to clobber our narrator with the truth behind this illusion. In truth, none of us can know that "we are real". We cannot trust our memories, because they are merely sensations played back to us--just in the same way that our fingertips relay truth about the surface beneath them, our memory systems relay truth about the subtle chemical markers left there by a past self, keening with desire to be heard, to be seen, to be remembered by a future conscious spark that dares to look back upon them.

We might as well all be Deckard, or Roy. How would we know? The conclusion in Blade Runner is that we simply don't. The only reason Roy or Deckard understand their existence as replicants is because the "rules" of private experience are violated. I would venture this particular point to anyone who concludes (after watching the Director's Cut) that Deckard is a replicant: If the Tyrell Corporation understands sufficiently the nature of memory in human brains to construct a structure such as a Nexus 6 replicant, then what is to say that Edward James Olmos' character isn't simply recounting data collected by studying Deckard's human brain?

I don't say this because I think Deckard is meant to be human. I say this to illustrate the completeness of the conundrum presented in this movie, and to relate it to the conundrum faced by our dear narrator as he stares down the ghost of Phaedrus, the father of the child our narrator is tasked to raise.

As a secular athiest, I don't see a "soul" hiding, complete and inviolable, inside us all. But when I read Robert Pirsig's seminal work, I look down at my body, feeling comforted. Not because our dear narrator convinces me of something new, presenting some large and over-arching philosophy of humankind that wipes away my fears of my mortality and the mutable nature of my "self" (such as it is). No, 'Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance' presents to me the raw, vulnerable, private sensations of existence that a secular atheist must clearly designate as, "these are sensations that happen to my brain and my scientific understanding of the world does not explain nor substantiate them".

And in so doing, it provides me with the truest, most palpable form of meaning that I have yet found in my three decades of life, most of which have been spent searching.

"This lump of matter over there feels these things too."

In this way, I feel that a very dear friend of mine has gone away, and I feel myself very much the worse off for his loss.

Rest in Peace, Robert. I will miss you.
